title: Ten things and one
hookLine: given ten things, one is held back, and he loses faith

lines: A SCENE AS PLAIN AS A SUM.
cards: A birthday. Ten presents on the table, every one chosen with care. The child opens nine, then ten, and asks: where's the eleventh?

The one I asked for? Suddenly the ten are forgotten, and the afternoon is about the one that isn't there. It's easy to laugh at that, and easy to do it, at thirty, at fifty, about a job, a body, a year.
Guru Arjan put that same arithmetic into Sukhmani more than four hundred years ago, plain as a sum.

teach.b: The stanza begins: das basatoo lai paachhai paavai. He takes ten things and puts them behind him. Das is ten; basatoo, things, gifts.
Paachhai paavai: puts them at his back, out of sight. Then: ek basat kaaran bikhot gavaavai. For the sake of one thing, he throws away his trust.
Commentators read that last word slightly differently, losing faith, losing credit, being shown as faithless, but the picture holds. Ten received, one withheld, and the ten disappear behind the one.
Ten against one isn't close. It's not a story about someone treated unfairly; it's about attention.
The missing thing sits in front of the eyes, and the ten slip behind the back, still there, still given, just unseen.

teach.h: ONE HELD BACK, AND TRUST GOES.
teach.b: That's why this stanza follows a salok about the Giver. The ingratitude it describes isn't loud or rude. It's quiet, ordinary, and it happens by turning around.
And the week ends here. Six days ago, the third ashtpadi asked for the Name and deeds to match.

Then the fourth: remember who made you; the ungrateful guest; the child calling out, You are mother and father, to You this prayer. Then the fifth: the Giver, the open palm, and now ten things and one.
The question is which way you're facing.

how: Sikhs read this stanza as part of Sukhmani Sahib, often daily; preachers in katha often use the ten-and-one picture to talk about gratitude.

games.q: you've been handed ten gifts. one thing you hoped for isn't there. in the stanza, what does the person do?
o: thank the giver for the ten.
put the ten behind his back and lose trust over the one.
games.why: das basatoo lai paachhai paavai: the ten go behind the back, and for one thing he throws his trust away.

practice: Count ten things you've been given on your fingers, small and real: the breath you're taking, water from a tap, someone who answered a message, your eyes, a bed.
If the missing thing pushes in, notice it and let it stand at the back for once; then rest your two full hands in your lap and breathe with them.

carryVoice: Your line: ten given, one held back. The table was full all along. A week, done.
